newsitem.title: GERMANY: Peru rebel in Germany sees violent end to crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel in Germany sees violent end to crisis.

text.p: The international spokesman for Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's house in Lima said on Saturday he thought the Peruvian government would end the crisis with violence.

"The Peruvian government has put things in place for a military solution. Journalists have been pushed aside and the residence has been surrounded by tanks," said Isaac Velazco, spokesman of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
Last night police tested how far they could push the rebels with night manoeuvres outside the residence, but there was no immediate response from inside the compund.

Velazco, speaking at a news conference before a public rally in the southern German city, said the MRTA knew their occupation would be answered with military action, but had acted to stop the killing of MRTA prisoners in Peru.
"MTRA fighters would rather die than continue to live on their knees," said Velazco, who is based in Germany.

Marxist rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on December 17, taking more than 500 hostages and demanding the release of some 400 imprisoned comrades and the end to the country's "neoliberal economic policy".

Velazco would not comment on whether he had been in contact with the rebels, who have released most of the hostages, but said they were ready to negotiate with the Peruvian government as long as their colleagues were set free.
Velazco addressed around 100 people at a public rally and called for a political solution to the conflict in Peru and freedom for political prisoners.
Velazco said a violent end to the crisis would deepen the conflict in Peru.
"The MRTA is ready to continue the war for as long as it takes to achieve political and social rights in Peru," he said.
Velazco said Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's comments that he wants to wipe out the MRTA once the crisis is over had led to uncertainty among the hostages.
Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is among the captives, has pledged not to storm the building unless one of the hostages is hurt.
The roughly 15 rebels in the house are armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers and have mined and booby-trapped the compound against possible attack.

Though both sides have said they are willing to sit down to discuss a peaceful end to the 39-day crisis, Fujimori has ruled out starting talks until the rebels drop their demand for the release of their comrades.

To pressure Fujimori, the MRTA continues to hold two Peruvian ministers, judges, congressmen, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
